# Task Overview

> We are going to re-analyse a dataset containing transcriptomic samples from healthy patients and patients infected with mycobacterium tuberculosis, which causes tuberculosis disease. This data has previously been analysed by [Singhania et al, 2018](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-04579-w). Tuberculosis is a heterogeneous disease with high global burden. Patients infected with mycobacterium tuberculosis can be classified as active or latent infections, depending on whether clinical symptoms are present or not. Diagnosing tuberculosis infection can be difficult, especially in asymptomatic patients with latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI). 

> Therefore, it would be beneficial to identify some biomarkers which can act as sensitive and specific indicators of the disease state. The data is open-access and available through the National Center for Biotechnology Information's Gene Expression Omnibus project. Data were collected from three cohorts (the London, South Africa, and Leicester cohorts).

>  The goal of this practical will be to perform an analysis of these data, using the principles learned in the lecture. Specifically, we will practice data pre-processing, normalisation, batch effect correction, data exploration with principal component analysis and hierarchical clustering, and differential gene expression analysis. 

# Data Management

## 0a) Set up your project

### Why do we need a project?

> When you analyse data in R, you need to tell R *where* files are. For example, you might load data into your environment by defining a path `"C:/Users/me/Documents/data/file.xlsx"`. However, this is problematic, since it is specific to your own computer setup. The code will then break as soon as you move the files, share them with a colleague, or re-run the analysis on a different machine. 

> To avoid this, we will introduce some basic organisational skills for an R project. Firstly, we will contain the work in a single **R project folder** (the root), and refer to every file *relative to that folder*. This makes specifying paths for loading data and saving outputs more robust.

> Using a project folder also helps to organise files in a clean way.
> - **raw data** : the original data files, which you should never modify;
> - **analysis** : the code (such as this `.Rmd` file) that reads the raw data and produces results;
> - **output** : everything the code creates (figures, tables, processed data), which should be able to be perfectly regenerated by re-running the code.

### Create the project folder

> 1. In RStudio, click `File > New Project... > New Directory > New Project`.
> 2. Give the project a name, for example `omics_practicals`, and choose where to save it on your computer. Click `Create Project`. 
> 3. RStudio restarts inside your new project. You can check this in the top-right corner of RStudio, which now shows the project name, and in the `Files` pane, which shows a single file called e.g. `omics_practicals.Rproj`.

> Next, create three sub-folders inside the project. In the `Files` pane of RStudio, click `New Folder` and create `data-raw`, `analysis`, and `output`. Alternatively, run the following code once in the R console.

```{r, eval = F}
dir.create("data-raw")
dir.create("analysis")
dir.create("output")
```

> Your project should now look like this:

```
omics_practicals/
├── omics_practicals.Rproj    <- marks the "root" of the project
├── data-raw/                 <- the 3 raw data files
├── analysis/                 <- this practical (.Rmd file)
└── output/                   <- figures and results that you save
```

### Add the files

> 1. Copy the three Excel files I sent you into the `data-raw` folder: `GSE107991_Raw_counts_Berry_London.xlsx`, `GSE107992_Raw_counts_Berry_SouthAfrica.xlsx`, and `GSE107993_Raw_counts_Leicester_non_progressor_longitudnal_only.xlsx`.
> 2. Copy this practical (the `.Rmd` file) into the `analysis` folder.
> 3. In the `Files` pane of RStudio, open the `analysis` folder and click on the `.Rmd` file to open it. 

> **Important:** always start your work by opening the project (double-click `omics_practicals.Rproj`, or use `File > Open Project`), and open the `.Rmd` file from *within* RStudio's `Files` pane. If you open the `.Rmd` file directly from your Downloads folder, it will not be part of the project and the paths below will not work.

### How do we refer to files?

> By default, R Markdown runs code from the folder where the `.Rmd` file is saved (here, `analysis/`), which would make paths confusing. Instead, we will use the `here` package. The function `here()` always returns the path to the root of your project (the folder containing the `.Rproj` file), wherever the code is run from. We then build paths from this root. For example, `here("data-raw", "my_file.xlsx")` points to `my_file.xlsx` inside the `data-raw` folder, and `here("output", "my_plot.png")` points to a file in the `output` folder. The same code works on any computer and operating system, and you never have to type a full path.

> The data come from the NCBI's Gene Expression Omnibus. [Here is the link](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE107995) for the series *A modular transcriptional signature identifies phenotypic heterogeneity of human tuberculosis infection*, which consists of the SubSeries `GSE107991`, `GSE107992`, and `GSE107993`. These SubSeries correspond to three different patient cohorts, called the London, South Africa, and Leicester cohorts, respectively. You do not need to download anything yourself: the raw count data are the files in your `data-raw` folder, and we will download the metadata directly in R below.

> In this first step, I will give you the code to load the data and merge it together to make it easier to work with. 

## 0d) Load data

> Load the raw counts data with the `read_excel()` function, using `here()` to build the path to each file.

```{r, message = F}
# Read the raw counts for the London data
london_raw <-
  read_excel(here("data-raw", "GSE107991_Raw_counts_Berry_London.xlsx"))

# Read the raw counts for the South Africa data
southafrica_raw <-
  read_excel(here("data-raw", "GSE107992_Raw_counts_Berry_SouthAfrica.xlsx"))

# Read the raw counts for the Leicester data
leicester_raw <-
  read_excel(here(
    "data-raw",
    "GSE107993_Raw_counts_Leicester_non_progressor_longitudnal_only.xlsx"
  ))
```


## 0e) Download metadata

> Use the `getGEO()` function from the `GEOquery` package to download the metadata corresponding to these files. 

```{r, results = 'hide', message = F}
# Load the metadata for the London, South Africa, and Leicester datasets
london_metadata <-
  GEOquery::getGEO("GSE107991", GSEMatrix = FALSE)  #London
southafrica_metadata <-
  GEOquery::getGEO("GSE107992", GSEMatrix = FALSE)  # SouthAfrica
leicester_metadata <-
  GEOquery::getGEO("GSE107993", GSEMatrix = FALSE)  #Leicester
```

## 0f) Process the metadata

> Extract relevant information from the metadata.

```{r}
# This function extracts the relevant columns from the metadata files and changes some of the names of the values
get_info <- function(i, meta) {
  name <- meta@gsms[[i]]@header$source_name_ch1
  name <- gsub("Active_TB", "ActiveTB", name)
  name <- gsub("Test_set", "TestSet", name)
  name <- gsub("Validation_set", "ValidationSet", name)
  name <- gsub("Non_progressor", "NonProgressor", name)
  res <- unlist(strsplit(name, split = "_"))
  res <- c(res, meta@gsms[[i]]@header$title)
  res
}

# Build a data frame of sample information (one row per sample) for one cohort
build_info_df <- function(meta) {
  infos <- sapply(seq_along(meta@gsms), FUN = get_info, meta = meta)
  infos_df <- cbind.data.frame(GSMID = names(meta@gsms), t(infos))
  rownames(infos_df) <- names(meta@gsms)
  infos_df
}

infos_df_london <- build_info_df(london_metadata)
colnames(infos_df_london)[-1] <-
  c("Cohort", "Location", "Set", "Status", "SampleName")

infos_df_southafrica <- build_info_df(southafrica_metadata)
colnames(infos_df_southafrica)[-1] <-
  c("Cohort", "Location", "Set", "Status", "SampleName")

# In the Leicester metadata, Status comes before Set, so we reorder the
# columns to match the other two cohorts
infos_df_leicester <- build_info_df(leicester_metadata)
colnames(infos_df_leicester)[-1] <-
  c("Cohort", "Location", "Status", "Set", "SampleName")
```

## 0g) Merge data

> Change the format to wide, so each column is a gene, and merge the data.

```{r}
# Bind the metadata for London, SA, and Leicester together
infos_all <-
  rbind.data.frame(infos_df_london, infos_df_southafrica, infos_df_leicester)

# Merge the counts for London, SA, and Leicester, matching on the first 3 columns
# (the gene identifiers : Genes, Gene_name, Gene_biotype)
counts_merged <-
  merge(
    x = merge(x = london_raw, y = southafrica_raw, by = c(1:3)),
    y = leicester_raw,
    by = c(1:3)
  ) %>% dplyr::select(-Gene_name, -Gene_biotype)

# Pivot to wide format : transpose so that samples are rows (the first row, which contains the gene names, is dropped)
counts_all <- t(counts_merged)[-1, ] %>% as.data.frame()

# Columns are genes
colnames(counts_all) <- counts_merged$Genes

# Rows are samples
rownames(counts_all) <- seq_len(nrow(counts_all))

# Now we merge the counts with the metadata by the sample name
merged_all <- merge(
  y = bind_cols("SampleName" = colnames(counts_merged)[-1], counts_all),
  x = infos_all,
  by = "SampleName"
) %>% distinct()

# The metadata columns of the merged dataframe
metadata_cols <- c("SampleName", "GSMID", "Cohort", "Location", "Set", "Status")

# Extract the counts and store them as numeric values in the dataframe
counts_all <- merged_all %>% 
  dplyr::select(-all_of(metadata_cols)) %>% 
  sapply(as.numeric) %>% 
  as.data.frame()

# Extract the metadata
metadata_all <- merged_all %>% 
  dplyr::select(all_of(metadata_cols))

# Visualise the start of the merged dataframe
merged_all[, c(1:8)] %>% 
  head(5)
```

# 1) Data pre-processing

## 1a) Remove unexpressed genes

> A typical pre-processing step is to remove genes which are unexpressed (or expressed at a constant level) in every sample, since these provide no information. Remove these genes from the data.

> How many genes do you remove with this step?

```{r}
# Extract the total counts for each gene
count_sums <- colSums(counts_all)

# Unexpressed genes are those without a single count across samples
unexpressed_genes <- colnames(counts_all)[count_sums == 0]

# Remove these from the data
counts_all_filtered <- counts_all %>% 
  dplyr::select(-all_of(unexpressed_genes))

# how many genes were removed?
message(paste0(
  unexpressed_genes %>% length(),
  " unexpressed genes removed from the data."
))
```

> **Answer:** 6,443 genes were removed from the data.

## 1b) Remove non-protein coding genes

> Many investigators only include protein-coding genes in their analysis. Information on whether a gene is protein coding or not may be found in the raw counts under the Gene_biotype columns. For example, the first biotype values for the London data are:

```{r}
london_raw$Gene_biotype %>% 
  head()
```

> Using this information, filter the counts to only include genes that are protein-coding. How many genes were removed in this stage?

```{r}
# Use the london data to extract the names of the protein-coding genes
non_protein_coding_genes <- london_raw %>%
  filter(Gene_biotype != "protein_coding") %>%
  pull(Genes)

# De-select non-protein-coding genes from the counts matrix
counts_all_filtered_proteincoding <- counts_all_filtered %>%
  dplyr::select(!any_of(non_protein_coding_genes))

# how many genes were removed?
message(paste0(
  intersect(non_protein_coding_genes, colnames(counts_all_filtered)) %>% length(),
  " non-protein-coding genes removed from the data."
))
```

> **Answer:** 32,221 genes were removed from the data.

> Now we are finished with the data loading and merging, we may remove all of the unnecessary data from the global environment using the `rm()` function. This is good practice when using high-dimensional data, as memory can quickly be occupied by large, unnecessary files in the global environment. 

```{r}
# Here we list the objects to keep
keep <- c("metadata_all",
    "counts_all_filtered_proteincoding")

# Remove everything else from the global environment
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), keep))

# Garbage collection to clear unused memory
invisible(gc())
```

# 2) Normalisation 

> Normalisation is a crucial step in RNA-seq analysis to ensure that samples are comparable. An important point here is that our data comes from 3 different studies (London, SA, and Leicester). Let's investigate the impact of this study variable on the data. 

## 2a) Investigate study effects

> The library size of a sample is the total number of counts across all genes. Compute the library sizes and visualise them on a bar chart using `ggplot2`. Colour the samples by the study from which it came. What do you notice? 

> Save this figure in your `output` folder using `ggsave()`, with `here()` to build the path (e.g. `here("output", "library_sizes.png")`). Use this practice for every figure you produce in this practical, ensuring that the saved figure has reasonable text sizes, axis names, etc. 

```{r}
# Create a new dataframe to store the library sizes, the sample identifier, and the study name
library_sizes <- data.frame(
  library_size = rowSums(counts_all_filtered_proteincoding),
  SampleName = metadata_all$SampleName,
  Location = metadata_all$Location
)

# Use ggplot to visualise these as a bar chart coloured by study
library_sizes_plot <-
  ggplot(library_sizes,
         aes(x = SampleName, y = library_size, fill = Location)) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Library Size") +
  ggtitle("Library Sizes by Sample and Location")

# Save the figure in the output folder
ggsave(
  filename = here("output", "library_sizes.png"),
  plot = library_sizes_plot,
  width = 10,
  height = 6
)

# Display the figure
library_sizes_plot
```

> **Answer:** There are differences in library size both between individuals and between studies. Therefore, these samples are not comparable without normalisation. 

## 2b) Log2-CPM normalisation

> In the lecture, we introduced a simple way to normalise data based on library size:log2-Counts-per-million (log2-CPM). This is calculated by first dividing each count by its sample's library size, then multiplying by a million, and finally taking a log2 transformation. 

> Using the `cpm()` (counts-per-million) function from the `edgeR` package with the `log = TRUE` argument, compute the log2-CPM of these data. 

> **Tip**: If you are unsure about how this function works, use the code ``?cpm()`` to bring up the documentation in the Help panel in Rstudio.

```{r}
dge <- t(counts_all_filtered_proteincoding)

# Convert the raw counts into Log2-CPM
counts_log2_cpm <-
  cpm(dge, log = TRUE) %>% 
  t() %>% 
  as.data.frame()
```

> As a sanity check, I recommend that you inspect the data and compare it to the non-normalised dataset to convince yourself that everything looks OK. 

> In the lecture, we introduced Principal component analysis (PCA) as a useful tool for representing high-dimensional data in a lower-dimensional space, while preseving signals which contribute to between-sample variability. 

> I will first demonstrate how to use the `prcomp()` function to perform a PCA on the non-normalised data. Note that, since PCA is sensitive to the scale of the data, it is important to center and scale the data (such that every variable has mean 0 and sd 1) using the arguments `center` and `scale.` arguments in `prcomp()`.

```{r}
# Perform PCA on the raw (filtered) counts
pca_res <-
  prcomp(counts_all_filtered_proteincoding,
         center = TRUE,
         scale. = TRUE)

# The coordinates projected into the principal component space can be extracted as
pc_coordinates = pca_res$x

# The columns of the objects correspond to the PCs, i.e. the values of the samples projected onto PC1 are
pc_coordinates[, 1] %>% 
  head()

# The proportion of variability explained by each PC can also be extracted with 
pc_prop_variability = summary(pca_res)$importance %>% 
  t() %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  dplyr::select(`Proportion of Variance`)

# For example, the proportion explained by the first PC is 
pc_prop_variability[1,]
```

> I will now demonstrate how we can visualise the data in a reduced dimension using the results of the PCA. In particular, we might be interested in how the study location (London, Leicester, or South Africa) contributes to variability in the data. To do this, we can visualise the samples projected onto the first 2 PCs and colour the points by the location. 

```{r}
# Extract PC1 and PC2 for plotting
pca_df <- data.frame(
  PC1 = pc_coordinates[, 1],
  PC2 = pc_coordinates[, 2],
  Location = metadata_all$Location,
  Sample = metadata_all$SampleName
)

# Plot PC1 and PC2, colour points by location
ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = Location)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PC1 (", round(pc_prop_variability[1,] * 100, 1), "%)"), # Annotation: percentage of variability explained by PC1
    y = paste0("PC2 (", round(pc_prop_variability[2,] * 100, 1), "%)"), # Annotation: percentage of variability explained by PC2
    color = "Location",
    title = "PCA of raw data"
  )
```

> What does this visualisation tell us?

> **Answer**: A large amount of variability in the data can be explained just by one variable. This is likely due to the strong influence of the Location variable, showing that a batch effect is present.  

> Now, use the example above to perform a PCA using the `prcomp()` function on the log2-CPM normalised data. Has this normalisation step removed the study-effect?

```{r}
# Perform PCA on the raw (filtered) counts
pca_res <-
  prcomp(counts_log2_cpm,
         center = TRUE,
         scale. = TRUE)

# The coordinates projected into the principal component space can be extracted as
pc_coordinates = pca_res$x

# The columns of the objects correspond to the PCs, i.e. the values of the samples projected onto PC1 are
pc_coordinates[, 1] %>% 
  head()

# The proportion of variability explained by each PC can also be extracted with 
pc_prop_variability = summary(pca_res)$importance %>% 
  t() %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  dplyr::select(`Proportion of Variance`)

# For example, the proportion explained by the first PC is 
pc_prop_variability[1,]

# Extract PC1 and PC2 for plotting
pca_df <- data.frame(
  PC1 = pc_coordinates[, 1],
  PC2 = pc_coordinates[, 2],
  Location = metadata_all$Location,
  Sample = metadata_all$SampleName
)

# Plot PC1 and PC2, colour points by location
ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = Location)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PC1 (", round(pc_prop_variability[1,] * 100, 1), "%)"), # Annotation: percentage of variability explained by PC1
    y = paste0("PC2 (", round(pc_prop_variability[2,] * 100, 1), "%)"), # Annotation: percentage of variability explained by PC2
    color = "Location",
    title = "PCA of log2-cpm data"
  )
```

> **Answer**: The batch effect is still present. In particular, the samples from the Leicester cohort are very separated from the others on PC1.

## 2c) Log2-CPM-TMM Normalisation

> Another typical normalisation approach is to use the *trimmed mean of M-values* (TMM) method. This calculates normalisation factors which exclude extreme values. This normalisation can be achieved through the following code. 

```{r}
# Make a DGEList object with the raw counts (genes in rows, so we transpose)
dge_list <- DGEList(t(counts_all_filtered_proteincoding))

# Calculate the normalisation factors with TMM
dge <- calcNormFactors(dge_list, method = "TMM")

# Convert the raw counts into Log2-CPM-TMM
counts_log2_cpm_tmm <-
  cpm(dge, log = TRUE) %>% 
  t() %>% 
  as.data.frame()
``` 

> Using your previous code, plot the points on the first two principal components, coloured by location. Has this normalisation step solved the problem?

```{r}
# Perform PCA on the raw (filtered) counts
pca_res <-
  prcomp(counts_log2_cpm_tmm,
         center = TRUE,
         scale. = TRUE)

# The coordinates projected into the principal component space can be extracted as
pc_coordinates = pca_res$x

# The columns of the objects correspond to the PCs, i.e. the values of the samples projected onto PC1 are
pc_coordinates[, 1] %>% 
  head()

# The proportion of variability explained by each PC can also be extracted with 
pc_prop_variability = summary(pca_res)$importance %>% 
  t() %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  dplyr::select(`Proportion of Variance`)

# For example, the proportion explained by the first PC is 
pc_prop_variability[1,]

# Extract PC1 and PC2 for plotting
pca_df <- data.frame(
  PC1 = pc_coordinates[, 1],
  PC2 = pc_coordinates[, 2],
  Location = metadata_all$Location,
  Sample = metadata_all$SampleName
)

# Plot PC1 and PC2, colour points by location
ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = Location)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PC1 (", round(pc_prop_variability[1,] * 100, 1), "%)"), # Annotation: percentage of variability explained by PC1
    y = paste0("PC2 (", round(pc_prop_variability[2,] * 100, 1), "%)"), # Annotation: percentage of variability explained by PC2
    color = "Location",
    title = "PCA of log2-cpm-TMM data"
  )
```

> **Answer:** Even after this normalisation, there is still a study effect, especially related to the Leicester location.

## 2d) Batch effect correction

> We can view the study as a batch variable, since we do not expect it to contribute much to the heterogeneity between samples. To correct for batch effects in RNA-seq data, we can use the *ComBat-Seq* method. We do this using the `ComBat_seq()` function from the `sva` package. 

> In this method, we must specify two things. Firstly, the batch variable (`Location`), and secondly, a variable whose effects we want to remain intact after correction (in this case, the `Status` variable, which provides information on the disease states of the patients). We apply *ComBat-Seq* to the raw, filtered counts to correct for the `batch = Location`, while keeping preserved effects from `group = metadata_all$Status` using the follow code (may take a couple of minutes). 

```{r}
# Run ComBat-Seq (it expects genes in rows, so we transpose)
counts_combat <-
  ComBat_seq(
    counts = t(counts_all_filtered_proteincoding),
    batch = metadata_all$Location,
    group = metadata_all$Status
  )
```

> Now that we have attempted to correct for the batch effect in the raw counts, use the previous code on this corrected matrix to normalise the data using Log2-CPM-TMM. Then, visualise the data on the first two PCs, as before, and conclude if there still remains a study effect in the data. 

```{r}
# Make a DGEList object with the raw counts
dge_list <- DGEList(counts_combat)

# Calculate the normalisation factors with TMM
dge <- calcNormFactors(dge_list, method = "TMM")

# Convert the raw counts into Log2-CPM-TMM
counts_combat_log2_cpm_tmm <-
  cpm(dge, log = TRUE) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame()

# Perform PCA on the raw (filtered) counts
pca_res <-
  prcomp(counts_combat_log2_cpm_tmm,
         center = TRUE,
         scale. = TRUE)

# The coordinates projected into the principal component space can be extracted as
pc_coordinates = pca_res$x

# The columns of the objects correspond to the PCs, i.e. the values of the samples projected onto PC1 are
pc_coordinates[, 1] %>% 
  head()

# The proportion of variability explained by each PC can also be extracted with 
pc_prop_variability = summary(pca_res)$importance %>% 
  t() %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  dplyr::select(`Proportion of Variance`)

# For example, the proportion explained by the first PC is 
pc_prop_variability[1,]

# Extract PC1 and PC2 for plotting
pca_df <- data.frame(
  PC1 = pc_coordinates[, 1],
  PC2 = pc_coordinates[, 2],
  Location = metadata_all$Location,
  Sample = metadata_all$SampleName
)

# Plot PC1 and PC2, colour points by location
ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = Location)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PC1 (", round(pc_prop_variability[1,] * 100, 1), "%)"), # Annotation: percentage of variability explained by PC1
    y = paste0("PC2 (", round(pc_prop_variability[2,] * 100, 1), "%)"), # Annotation: percentage of variability explained by PC2
    color = "Location",
    title = "PCA of ComBat-Seq corrected log2-cpm-TMM data"
  )
```

> **Answer**: the batch effect appears to have been mitigated.

> Since we have finished with the pre-processing, here we can remove all useless data from the global environment. 

```{r}
# Here we list the objects to keep
keep <-
  c("metadata_all",
    "counts_combat_log2_cpm_tmm",
    "counts_combat")

# Remove everything else from the global environment
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), keep))

# Garbage collection to clear unused memory
invisible(gc())
```

# 3) Data Exploration

> Now that we have preprocessed the data and (hopefully) removed any batch effects, we can start to explore it. The goal is to use tools like PCA and hierarchical clustering to explore any obvious signals in the data related to the patient status. 

## 3a) Principal Component Analysis 

> Perform a PCA to explore whether the variability in the gene expression data can be explained by the disease status of patients. Like before, perform a PCA on the batch-corrected-Log2-CPM-TMM-normalised data and plot the data on the first two PCs. However, this time, colour the points by their disease status. What does this suggest? 

```{r}
# Perform PCA on the raw (filtered) counts
pca_res <-
  prcomp(counts_combat_log2_cpm_tmm,
         center = TRUE,
         scale. = TRUE)

# The coordinates projected into the principal component space can be extracted as
pc_coordinates = pca_res$x

# The columns of the objects correspond to the PCs, i.e. the values of the samples projected onto PC1 are
pc_coordinates[, 1] %>% 
  head()

# The proportion of variability explained by each PC can also be extracted with 
pc_prop_variability = summary(pca_res)$importance %>% 
  t() %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  dplyr::select(`Proportion of Variance`)

# For example, the proportion explained by the first PC is 
pc_prop_variability[1,]

# Extract PC1 and PC2 for plotting
pca_df <- data.frame(
  PC1 = pc_coordinates[, 1],
  PC2 = pc_coordinates[, 2],
  Status = metadata_all$Status,
  Sample = metadata_all$SampleName
)

# Plot PC1 and PC2, colour points by Status
ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = Status)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PC1 (", round(pc_prop_variability[1,] * 100, 1), "%)"), # Annotation: percentage of variability explained by PC1
    y = paste0("PC2 (", round(pc_prop_variability[2,] * 100, 1), "%)"), # Annotation: percentage of variability explained by PC2
    color = "Status",
    title = "PCA of ComBat-Seq corrected log2-cpm-TMM data by disease status"
  )
```

> **Answer**: The samples with active tuberculosis seem to systematically vary from the others, suggesting that this disease state is contributing to some of the variability observed in the data.

## 3b) Hierarchical clustering

> In addition, we can explore signal in the data using hierarchical clustering algorithms. Here, the goal is to determine which samples are similar and which are different. If these similarities and/or differences can be explained by the disease state, it suggests a signal might be present. 

> To perform hierarchical clustering, we need three inputs: dataset, distance function defining similariy 
> - dataset
> - distance metric, defining similarity between data points
> - linkage function, describing similarity between clusters

> In this first example, I will demonstrate how we can do agglomerative hierarchical clustering on the gene expression using *Euclidean distance* and *complete linkage*, and plot the results as a dendrogram. First, we extract the sample names and disease statuses for later

```{r}
# Extract the sample names
sample_names <- metadata_all$SampleName

# Extract the disease states
Status <- metadata_all$Status
```

> We can now compute the distances between the samples using the `dist()` function. 

```{r}
distance_matrix <-
  dist(counts_combat_log2_cpm_tmm, method = "euclidean")
```

> Then, we can use the `hclust()` function from the `flashClust` package to perform agglomerative hierarchical clustering based on these distances. 

```{r}
# Perform complete linkage hierarchical clustering with hclust()
hclust_result <- hclust(distance_matrix, method = "complete")
```

> A dendrogram can be plotted with the `as.dendrogram()` function. I will also use some code to plot this with the sample labels coloured by the `Status` variable. 

> Do you notice any patterns? Is there any obvious way to determine the number of clusters in this case?

```{r}
# Compute the dendrogram
dend <- as.dendrogram(hclust_result)

# Compute the ordering of the sample labels
dend_labels_order <- order.dendrogram(dend)

# Reorder sample names and Status according to the dendrogram order
ordered_sample_names <- sample_names[dend_labels_order]
ordered_Status <- Status[dend_labels_order]

# Set the labels of the dendrogram to the ordered sample names
labels(dend) <- ordered_sample_names

# Convert dendrogram to a format suitable for ggplot2
dend_data <- dendro_data(dend)

label_data <- data.frame(label = ordered_sample_names,
                         Status = ordered_Status,
                         x = dend_data$labels$x)

# Create the dendrogram plot with ggplot2, ensuring proper label order
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = dend_data$segments, aes(
    x = x,
    y = y,
    xend = xend,
    yend = yend
  )) +
  geom_text(
    data = label_data,
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = 0,
      label = label,
      color = Status
    ),
    hjust = 1,
    vjust = 0.5,
    angle = 90,
    size = 3
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(
    title = "Hierarchical clustering of samples (euclidean distance, complete linkage)",
    x = "Samples",
    y = "Height",
    color = "Status"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
```

> **Answer**: some of the red samples (activeTB) tend to cluster together, although these clusters are not too distinct. This makes sense given what we previously observed with the PCA, which revealed the status to contribute to the variability in the data, but not hugely so.

> Try changing the `method` argument in the `hclust()` call to `method = "ward"`. Use the previous code to plot the dendrogram as before. A criterion to select the number of clusters which often accompanies the ward method is to select the number of clusters such that the next jump in the tree is the greatest. How many clusters would you choose with this criterion? What is your conclusion now?

```{r}
# Extract the sample names
sample_names <- metadata_all$SampleName

# Extract the disease states
Status <- metadata_all$Status

# Perform hierarchical clustering
# Compute the Euclidean distance matrix
distance_matrix <-
  dist(counts_combat_log2_cpm_tmm, method = "euclidean")

# Perform Ward hierarchical clustering with hclust()
hclust_result <- hclust(distance_matrix, method = "ward")

# Compute the dendrogram
dend <- as.dendrogram(hclust_result)

# Compute the ordering of the sample labels
dend_labels_order <- order.dendrogram(dend)

# Reorder sample names and Status according to the dendrogram order
ordered_sample_names <- sample_names[dend_labels_order]
ordered_Status <- Status[dend_labels_order]

# Set the labels of the dendrogram to the ordered sample names
labels(dend) <- ordered_sample_names

# Convert dendrogram to a format suitable for ggplot2
dend_data <- dendro_data(dend)

label_data <- data.frame(label = ordered_sample_names,
                         Status = ordered_Status,
                         x = dend_data$labels$x)

# Create the dendrogram plot with ggplot2, ensuring proper label order
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = dend_data$segments, aes(
    x = x,
    y = y,
    xend = xend,
    yend = yend
  )) +
  geom_text(
    data = label_data,
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = 0,
      label = label,
      color = Status
    ),
    hjust = 1,
    vjust = 0.5,
    angle = 90,
    size = 3
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(title = "Hierarchical clustering of samples (Ward linkage)", x = "Samples", y = "Height", color = "Status") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
```

> **Answer**: Now the samples appear to cluster together more strongly by status. A large jump in the tree can be observed between around 600 and 800 distance. Therefore, using this method, we would cut the tree at the last jump, resulting in two clusters.

```{r}
  c("metadata_all",
    "counts_combat_log2_cpm_tmm",
    "counts_combat")

# Remove everything else from the global environment
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), keep))

# Garbage collection to clear unused memory
invisible(gc())
```

# 4) Differential Gene Expression Analysis

> We are interested in identifying any genes whose expression is different between different disease states. For the purposes of this exercise, we will group together control and latent tuberculosis patients together, and compare them to the active infection group. We will use multiple methods to do this, and compare their results at the end. 

## 4a) EdgeR

> We will be following the edgeR pipeline, [found here](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/edgeR/inst/doc/edgeRUsersGuide.pdf).

> edgeR starts with raw integer counts. We can use the counts from ComBat-Seq (prior to normalisation). Starting from a DGEList object, follow the edgeR pipeline. This starts with estimating TMM normalisation factors with `calcNormFactors()`. Then, we estimate a common dispersion using `estimateCommonDisp()`. The negative binomial model can be fit with `glmQLFit()`. P-values can be extracted with `glmQLFTest()`, and the top genes can be extracted using the `topTags()` function. 

> Extract a vector of gene names which have adjusted p-value < 0.05, as well as |log2-fold-change| > 1. How many genes are differentially expressed according to this criterion?

```{r}
# Define a new column testGroup which groups together LTBI and control patients into one control group
metadata_all <- metadata_all %>%
  mutate(testGroup = recode_factor(Status, "LTBI" = "Control")) %>%
  relocate(testGroup, .after = Status)

# Define a DGEList object with the ComBat-Seq corrected counts
dge <-
  DGEList(counts = counts_combat,
          group = metadata_all$testGroup)

# Calculate normalisation factors with TMM
dge <- calcNormFactors(dge, method = "TMM")

# Specify a design matrix
design <- model.matrix(~ testGroup, data = metadata_all)

# Estimate common dispersion factors
dge_edgeR_common <- estimateCommonDisp(dge, design)

# Fit the quasi-likelihood GLM
fit_edgeR <- glmQLFit(dge_edgeR_common, design)

# Perform the test (coef = 2 compares ActiveTB to control)
qlf <- glmQLFTest(fit_edgeR, coef = 2)

# Store results in a dataframe and store significant gene names
results_edgeR <- topTags(qlf, n = Inf) %>% as.data.frame()

genelist_edgeR <- results_edgeR %>%
  filter(FDR < 0.05, abs(logFC) > 1) %>%
  rownames()

# How many genes were significantly differentially expressed?
message(paste0(
  genelist_edgeR %>% length(),
  " differentially expressed genes found."
))
```

> **Answer** 2,561 differentially expressed genes were found. 

> Repeat the previous experiment, but instead of estimating a common dispersion factor, estimate one for each gene using the `estimateDisp()` function. Do the results change significantly? 

```{r}
# Estimate a dispersion for each gene
dge_edgeR_genewise <- estimateDisp(dge, design)

# Fit the quasi-likelihood GLM
fit_edgeR_genewise <- glmQLFit(dge_edgeR_genewise, design)

# Perform the test (coef = 2 compares ActiveTB to control)
qlf_genewise <- glmQLFTest(fit_edgeR_genewise, coef = 2)

# Store results in a dataframe and store significant gene names
results_edgeR_genewise <-
  topTags(qlf_genewise, n = Inf) %>% as.data.frame()

genelist_edgeR_genewise <- results_edgeR_genewise %>%
  filter(FDR < 0.05, abs(logFC) > 1) %>%
  rownames()

# How many genes were significantly differentially expressed?
message(paste0(
  genelist_edgeR_genewise %>% length(),
  " differentially expressed genes found."
))

# How many significant genes were shared when estimating common vs gene-wise dispersion parameters?
message(
  intersect(genelist_edgeR_genewise, genelist_edgeR) %>% length(),
  " commonly differentially expressed genes found between the two methods."
)
```

> **Answer** 2,534 differentially expressed genes were found, which is not too different. 

## 4b) Voom-Limma

> Now, we will perform the same task using voom-limma. A tutorial can be [found here](https://ucdavis-bioinformatics-training.github.io/2018-June-RNA-Seq-Workshop/thursday/DE.html).

> Following the guide, apply the Voom-limma pipeline with the functions `voom()`, `lmFit()`, `eBayes()` and `decideTests()`. The output should be a vector giving the names of the differentially expressed genes defined by adjusted p-value < 0.05 and |log2-fold-change| > 1. How many genes are differentially expressed?

```{r}
# Define a DGEList object with the ComBat-Seq corrected counts
dge <-
  DGEList(counts = counts_combat,
          group = metadata_all$testGroup)

# Calculate normalisation factors with TMM
dge <- calcNormFactors(dge, method = "TMM")

# Specify a design matrix
design <- model.matrix( ~ testGroup, data = metadata_all)

# Use the voom() function to estimate the mean-variance relationship
v <- voom(dge, design, plot = TRUE)

# Fit the linear models to the data
fit_voom <- lmFit(v, design)

# Perform empirical Bayes tests
fit_voom <- eBayes(fit_voom, robust = TRUE)

# Count the up- and down-regulated genes (adjusted p-value < 0.05, |log2FC| > 1)
voomlimma_signif <-
  decideTests(fit_voom,
              adjust.method = "BH",
              p.value = 0.05,
              lfc = 1)
summary(voomlimma_signif)

# Put the results in a dataframe and find significant gene names
results_voom <- topTable(fit_voom, coef = 2, n = Inf) %>% as.data.frame()

genelist_voomlimma <- results_voom %>% filter(adj.P.Val < 0.05, abs(logFC) > 1) %>% rownames()

# How many genes were significantly differentially expressed?
message(paste0(
  genelist_voomlimma %>% length(),
  " differentially expressed genes found."
))
```

> **Answer** 738 differentially expressed genes were found. 

## 4c) dearseq

> Finally we will apply the dearseq pipeline. A guide can be [found here](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/dearseq/inst/doc/dearseqUserguide.html).

> Use the `dear_seq()` function to perform differential expression analysis. Since log2-fold-change values are not directly available from the dearseq package, you may use the ones calculated by `edgeR`. 

```{r}
res_dearseq <-
  dear_seq(
    # Log2-CPM-TMM data, with genes in rows
    exprmat = as.matrix(t(counts_combat_log2_cpm_tmm)),
    # The variable to test (ActiveTB vs control)
    variables2test = design[, "testGroupActiveTB", drop = FALSE],
    # The variables to adjust for (here, only the intercept)
    covariates = design[, "(Intercept)", drop = FALSE],
    which_test = "asymptotic",
    # The data are already normalised and log2-transformed
    preprocessed = TRUE
  )

# Extract the log2FC from the edgeR analysis (same gene order as the dearseq input)
logFC <- qlf$table$logFC
names(logFC) <- rownames(qlf$table)

# Compute significantly DE genes
dearseq_signif <- res_dearseq$pvals$adjPval < 0.05 & abs(logFC) > 1

genelist_dearseq <- names(dearseq_signif[dearseq_signif == TRUE])

# How many genes were significantly differentially expressed?
message(paste0(
  genelist_dearseq %>% length(),
  " differentially expressed genes found."
))
```

> **Answer** 618 differentially expressed genes were found. 

## 4d) Volcano plot

> A common representation of the results of DGEA is in the form of a so-called [*volcano plot*](https://olvtools.com/en/rnaseq/help/volcano-plot). The x-axis of a volcano plot is the log2FC value and the y-axis is the adjusted p-values on the log10 scale, with the axis inverted such that smaller p-values are greater on the y-axis. Typically, the ad-hoc limits which define differential expression (e.g. adjusted p-value < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1 in our case) are represented by lines on the plot. Significantly up-regulated genes are coloured as red and significantly down-regulated genes as blue. Sometimes, the few most significant genes are given labels showing their name. 

> Choose one of your analysis pipelines, and make a volcano plot to represent the results. Annotate the top 10 most significantly differentially expressed genes (by adjusted p-value) on the plot. 

```{r}
# EdgeR volcano plot
volcano_results <- results_edgeR %>% mutate(gene_name = rownames(results_edgeR)) %>% dplyr::select(gene_name, FDR, logFC)

volcano_results <- volcano_results %>%
  mutate(
    expression = case_when(
      FDR < 0.05 & logFC > 1 ~ "Up-regulated",
      FDR < 0.05 & logFC < -1 ~ "Down-regulated",
      TRUE ~ "Not significant"
    )
  )

top_10_genes <- volcano_results %>%
  filter(expression != "Not significant") %>%
  arrange(FDR) %>%
  head(10)

volcano_plot <-
  volcano_results %>% ggplot(aes(
    x = logFC,
    y = -log10(FDR),
    color = expression
  )) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Up-regulated" = "red",
    "Down-regulated" = "blue",
    "Not significant" = "grey"
  )) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(-1, 1),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = -log10(0.05),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Volcano Plot of Differential Gene Expression",
    x = "log2 Fold Change",
    y = "-log10 Adjusted P-value",
    color = "Expression"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))

# Add gene name annotations for top 10 genes
volcano_plot <- volcano_plot +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = top_10_genes,
    aes(label = gene_name),
    size = 3,
    box.padding = 0.5,
    point.padding = 0.5,
    force = 10,
    segment.color = "grey50"
  )

volcano_plot
```

## 4e) Results comparison

> Finally let's make some visualisations to compare the results from the 3 pipelines (voom-limma, edgeR and dearseq).

> First, use the `VennDiagram` package to visualise the agreement between the methods. 

```{r}
# Stop VennDiagram from writing a log file in the working directory
futile.logger::flog.threshold(futile.logger::ERROR, name = "VennDiagramLogger")

# Create a Venn Diagram
venn.plot <- venn.diagram(
  x = list(
    Voomlimma = genelist_voomlimma,
    EdgeR = genelist_edgeR,
    dearseq = genelist_dearseq
  ),
  category.names = c("Voom-Limma", "EdgeR", "dearseq"),
  filename = NULL,
  output = TRUE,
  fill = c("red", "blue", "green"),  # Colour of each set
  alpha = 0.5,                       # Transparency of the fills
  lwd = 2,                           # Line width of the circles
  col = "black",                     # Line colour of the circles
  cex = 2,                           # Text size
  fontface = "bold",                 # Bold text
  fontfamily = "sans"
)

# plot the Venn diagram in a new page
grid.newpage()  # Ensure the plot starts fresh
grid.draw(venn.plot)
```

> How many genes are identified by all three methods? Do the methods broadly agree?

```{r}
# Genes identified by all three methods
genes_all_methods <- Reduce(intersect,
                            list(genelist_voomlimma, genelist_edgeR, genelist_dearseq))

message(paste0(
  length(genes_all_methods),
  " genes were identified by all three methods."
))
```

> **Answer**: 455 genes were identified by all three methods. In particular, edgeR identifies a large amount of distinct genes. 

> An alternative way to visualise agreement is with a so-called UpSet plot. This representation works well when the number of classes to compare is greater than 3, such that a Venn diagram becomes hard to view. Using the `UpSetR` package, make an UpSet diagram. Do our 3 pipelines have concordant results? Make a conclusion about the sensitivity of the results to the choice of method. 

```{r}
# Now for the UpSet diagram, make one list of DEGs
gene_lists <- list(dearseq = genelist_dearseq,
                   voom = genelist_voomlimma,
                   edgeR = genelist_edgeR)

# Get all unique genes across the three lists
all_genes <-
  unique(c(genelist_dearseq, genelist_voomlimma, genelist_edgeR))

# Create a binary matrix to indicate the presence of each gene in each list
upset_data <- data.frame(
  dearseq = as.numeric(all_genes %in% genelist_dearseq),
  voom = as.numeric(all_genes %in% genelist_voomlimma),
  edgeR = as.numeric(all_genes %in% genelist_edgeR)
)

# Set the row names to be the gene names
rownames(upset_data) <- all_genes

# Generate the UpSet plot
upset(
  upset_data,
  sets = c("dearseq", "voom", "edgeR"),
  # Specify the sets you are comparing
  nsets = 3,
  # Number of sets to show
  order.by = "freq",
  # Order by frequency of overlaps
  empty.intersections = "on",
  # Include empty intersections
  main.bar.color = "black",
  # Color of the bars
  sets.bar.color = c("red", "green", "blue")  # Color for each set
)
```

> **Answer**: Although some of the results contain many shared genes, there are also a significant amount which are unique to a given method, suggesting sensitivity of the results to the choice of method. It may be beneficial to apply multiple methods to the same data and compare the results.
